items.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: the very first tune was a blues thing that Charlie Shavers had written... he did this kind of a test with all the guys that played solo in the band, like DeFranco and Charlie Shavers and Ziggy and all.

ctx.x: And in 1946, I had noticed this note and I wrote, the following band leaders called it quits: Woody Herman, Benny Goodman, Harry James, Les Brown, Benny Carter, Jack Teagarden, and so forth and so on. Was this something you guys noticed?

No I don’t think they called it quits — I think the big band era started to go in actually about ’48. When I got out of the Army I mean and I had the chance to audition for Les Paul, who at the time had a jazz trio. And I went up and luckily, thanks to my teacher and the technique he taught me you know, I could keep up with Les. And his idea of a ballad was about here [claps]. So I played with the group. We started at a place called the Rounders Club, which was literally at the corner of Sunset and Vine at the…

whether my reading ability, that would be like the first studio work, working on a radio show. That’s what I wanted to do eventually. items.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999
items.q: I used to be Charlie Shaver’s bodyguard when we did a tour of the south.

ctx.x: It seems like you’ve had some very fortunate working situations throughout your career that really gave you what you needed for the rest of your career.

Yeah. Well I said I’ve been lucky I’ve been able to play with all the people that I used to look up to when I was a teenager. Like I thought Basie was the greatest thing in life and when I was in the Army, one of the bass players in the Army, Walt Yoder had worked with Woody’s band and he knew all the guys in the Basie band and he took me and the guitar player, my best friend Tony Rizzi, out to the ballroom to see Basie, and he arranged for us to sit in. I mean I’m like 20 years old and Basie’s one of my idols,…

along in the business to avoid any of the pitfalls you might have run into, you should do it. You owe that to this business. Don’t get into racial scenes. I used to be Charlie Shaver’s bodyguard when we did a tour of the south. I mean I would go to the men’s room with him.
